speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Marchand (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION
subtopic: SMOLJAN, IVANCEV AND BILIC-DEPORTATION OF DESERTERS FROM YUGOSLAV VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to answer the question put to me yesterday by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. As it is a long answer I wish to make it at this stage in the proceedings.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition inquired yesterday about three Yugoslav ship deserters, Slavko Smoljan, Ante Ivancev, and Martin Bilic. He asked particularly why Bilic is to be allowed to remain in Canada under minister's permit while Smoljan and Ivancev are to be deported.
Martin Bilic deserted a Yugoslav ship at Sorel, Quebec, on July 28, 1966. He has four years elementary school, four years high school, and three years training in a trade school for auto mechanics, all of which he completed at the age of 19. At the immigration inquiry he claimed that his father had been killed by the communists and that his brother had been punished for attempting to escape to Italy. For this reason, and because of his qualifications, it was decided to allow him to remain in Canada under minister's permit.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Slavko Smoljan deserted the S.S. Caer-navon at Montreal, December 15, 1965, on his fourth trip to Canada as a crew member. He left school at the age of 15 and subsequently trained as a waiter. He went to sea as a
fisherman and later spent two years in the Yugoslav navy. He joined his ship in the United Kingdom in August 1965, after leaving Yugoslavia legally with a passport valid to December 1966. At the immigration inquiry he produced no evidence that he would be subject to persecution if he returned to Yugoslavia. The Immigration Appeal Board, in dismissing his appeal, recommended that he be deported.
Ante Ivancev deserted the S.S. Caernavon at Montreal on December 15, 1965. He left school at the age of 16 and subsequently trained as a waiter. He worked as a waiter in hotels in Yugoslavia until he secured a passport in August 1965, valid to December 1966, and went to France under a tourist visa. From France he went to the United Kingdom to join the ship from which he deserted in December, the same ship incidentally which brought Smoljan to Canada. At the immigration inquiry, Ivancev produced no evidence that he would be subject to persecution if he returned to Yugoslavia. The Immigration Appeal Board, in dismissing his appeal, recommended that he be deported.
It will be evident to hon. members that the case of Martin Bilic differs substantially from the cases of Smoljan and Ivancev. Bilic has qualifications which probably would have enabled him to qualify as an unsponsored immigrant, had it been possible to examine him in Yugoslavia. The other two do not have such qualifications. There is at least the possibility, moreover, however remote it may be, that Bilic might be persecuted for political reasons if he returned to his own country, whereas Smoljan and Ivancev quite clearly can make no such claim. Both of them had an opportunity to seek political asylum in at least one other country if that had been their real aim in leaving Yugoslavia.
I might say, finally, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian embassy in Yugoslavia has reported that the authorities there do not permit persons with political backgrounds, or evaders of military service, to serve on ocean-going ships from which defection would be relatively easy. This would appear to reduce considerably the possibility that ship deserters come within the categories of persons likely to be persecuted following their deportation to

December 6, 1966
Inquiries of the Ministry Yugoslavia. Thus far In 1966, 21 ship deserters have been deported, and there is no evidence whatever that anything untoward has happened to any of them. None the less, as in the case of Martin Bilic, we will continue to pay close attention to even the possibility that a particular individual might be subject to persecution.
This is not the first time deserters from ships have been deported to Yugoslavia. Some were deported in 1960, others in 1961 and 1962 when the Leader of the Opposition was prime minister of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: IMMIGRATION

speechtext:
That may have been so at times but not in the circumstances which have arisen in these cases. The minister has added to the cloud of doubt which surrounds the actions of his department.
He endeavours to differentiate between Bilic and these two persons who are to be deported. If there is one thing we must guard against in this country it is bureaucratic dictation which interferes with human rights. I want to say at once that the explanation given by the minister is transparent. He said neither of these two men who are being deported has produced any evidence that he would be persecuted if he returned to Yugoslavia. What manner of nonsense is that? Are they going to know in anticipation what is going to happen to them? I say that the explanation given is the usual explanation to cover up and conceal, and I take the strongest objection to action that will deny political refuge in this country to those who want to come to Canada, unless they have records that would make them unsuitable and unsatisfactory as immigrants.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that our Canadian representative in London is chairman of the sanctions committee for Rhodesia, and in view of the fact that a meeting has been called and the various representatives of the Commonwealth countries have been in communication with their respective governments, I wonder whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs could tell us whether or not our representative, the High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, has been in contact with him, and what policy Canada is adopting in respect of the critical situation which presently is developing around the matter of the compulsory sanctions requested of the United Nations by Mr. Wilson.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNITED NATIONS
subtopic: RHODESIA-CANADIAN POSITION ON APPLICATION OF SANCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend is aware the British Prime Minister has indicated the intention of the British government to move in the Security Council for sanctions under chapter 7 of the charter of the United Nations. The Sanctions committee under the chairmanship of the High Commissioner for Canada met this morning. As of this hour I cannot say whether or not the meeting has concluded. Of course the government has given him instructions concerning the position he should take at this meeting. I should like to remind my hon. friend that on November 24 the Prime Minister stated that Canada is committed to supporting selective mandatory sanctions under chapter 7 of the charter. This will be the position the government will take, depending on the action taken by the Security Council itself when it meets very shortly.

I hope that between now and the time the plans actually come into effect the minister will have consultation with the provinces, and the provinces and the minister will agree upon what paramedical services will be provided. Then, I hope the governor in council will be prepared to set forth by regulation, or by clauses contained in the agreements with the provinces, what these paramedical services are. I would make a special plea that optometric services be included because of the importance of these services to children and elderly people. I have seen many instances where children have been handicapped for life because of the lack of optometric services when they were small; and most old people now require optometric care. Consequently this is a very essential service.
There are other services which need to be included. I hope that what we are now passing will not be merely a pious wish, and that the minister will, if the provinces request it, be prepared to add some of these paramedical services to the present plan contained in Bill No. C-227.

In the application of this act to a plan established by an act of the legislature of a province-
I take it this means that the governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister, can extend paramedical services in a plan in a particular province even though other

provinces have not asked for a similar extension. If that is the interpretation of this amendment, and it certainly is mine, I would be glad to hear the minister say so. I am sure it would be a great improvement to the legislation, because I believe the minister not only wants flexibility as to services he can add, but flexibility so that he can keep abreast of the most progressive provinces-those that are prepared to move most rapidly. No province that wants to provide additional services ought to have to wait until other provinces catch up. As a matter of fact, the ability of some provinces to move more rapidly and introduce additional services will break new ground and will lead to the gathering of useful statistical data upon which other provinces can determine whether they want to follow the lead.
I hope the minister's interpretation is the same as my own, namely, that any province will be able to go ahead with providing additional services, provided of course that the minister and the governor in council agree.

speechtext:
I wish to say a few words about the administrative costs of carrying out this plan. The administration, in my opinion, should be part of the cost of the health care service. As defined in this act, the federal

December 6, 1966
Medicare
government will pay nothing whatsoever toward the cost of administration. I feel that with spending in the municipalities and provinces mushrooming, with their financial picture as it now is, the federal government ought to pay 50 per cent of the administration costs. I say this because the premier of Ontario, speaking one week ago in Toronto, said that the province would be hard put to find money and that the costs of provincial governments across Canada are mounting more quickly than the costs of the federal government. Provincial governments are having to spend money at a faster rate than the federal government is having to spend it. I hope I have made myself clear on this point. The provincial governments are more in need of money than is the federal government. The same thing applies to the municipalities.
The minister, I am sure, will know whether what the premier of Ontario said is correct. The premier of Ontario was not contradicted when he said that the need for money was greater in the provincial than in the federal field. I urge the minister to consider paying 50 per cent of the cost of administration. I also urge him to consider something else.
In estimating the costs of the plan, as I understand it the minister is taking 50 per cent of total medical costs from the Atlantic to the Pacific. In other words, the minister is taking an average. The minister must be aware that in Ontario, where I come from, medical costs are higher than in some other provinces; in British Columbia, they are also higher than in some other provinces. That applies also to Alberta. The minister, in estimating his costs, is taking an average and is saying, "We shall pay 50 per cent of that". This, to me, is misleading.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
It seems to me that when the government says it is paying 50 per cent of those costs, it is making a misleading statement. According to the original figures, the cost per capita across Canada amounted to $28. As the minister knows very well, that is not the situation today; the cost per capita has gone up to $35 or more. But taking the original figure of $28, the federal government undertook to pay $14 per capita. Today, in the province of Ontario medical costs are in the region of $35 to $40 per capita. So, in effect, we are asking the taxpayers of Ontario to pay a great deal more than the federal government. The actual cost at the time the original figures were prepared was around $34. So the federal government will, in effect, be paying $14 while asking 
Ontario to pay $20. When the government says it intends to pay 50 per cent of the cost, I do not think that is right. We should pay 50 per cent of the actual cost, and not leave the taxpayer in the province to carry an unfair proportion.
This applies to administration, also. Some of our provinces are not so well fixed financially as are others, and I suggest the federal government should make grants in order that we may know what the score is across Canada. Otherwise, our bookkeeping will be mixed up. We say we are paying 50 per cent but in fact we are only paying 42 per cent, or 45 per cent, whatever the figure is. I do not think this is right, because some of the high-cost provinces have their difficulties, too. In my own province of Ontario the government has resorted to deficit financing. There is a health resources fund there, and the province has to match federal expenditures dollar for dollar. Where will the province get the money to put up buildings and furnish them as it should? It does not have the borrowing power of the federal authority. If I interpret the statements of the premier of Ontario correctly, the result will be that his administration will need to consider very carefully the funds available for education, and in the field of health and welfare. Surely, this would be a retrograde step at a time when medicare is being introduced.
For these reasons, I believe the government should seriously consider accepting responsibility for 50 per cent of the administrative costs and 50 per cent of the actual cost of the scheme in a province, not across the dominion. Only in this way will some provinces be able to devote sufficient funds to the health resources plan, the purpose of which is to furnish and equip the buildings which will be necessary to enable the doctors and the paramedical services to do their work. The stipulation is that the federal government will put up one dollar for every dollar provided by the province. If the province does not have those dollars available, how is it to proceed with the construction of the medical centres which are needed for medicare? I urge the minister to give this matter careful consideration.

maintopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
I should like to add my voice to that of my hon. friend from Simcoe East in asking that the minister consider another definition of the 50 per cent assistance to be given to the provinces in connection with this medicare program.
The costs which have to be borne differ from province to province. In some areas the
December G, 196G

cost is higher than in others. We, in the province of Ontario, are faced with higher costs than are most other provinces. The minister should remember that half the money raised for this and other such schemes is raised in the province of Ontario. We do not want to brag about that; we are always ready to assist other provinces out of the funds we raise and contribute to the federal government. But we do feel, bearing in mind that the cost of medical services and so on is higher in Ontario than elsewhere, that the equitable way would be to proceed on the basis of 50 per cent of provincial costs, not 50 per cent of the cost on a national average. If this were done, each province would get the money to which it is entitled from the federal government.
This is only fair. The 50 per cent contribution based on a national average might almost pay the actual cost of some of our provinces, whTe in other provinces it would not nearly approach the cost of the services provided. So,
I ask the minister whether it would not be possible for h'm to define this 50 per cent contribution to the provinces in different terms, both with respect to the administration and to the other costs, in order that its application would be fairer for all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would deal with th s important question which has been raised by my hon. friends from Simcoe East and Wellington-Huron.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport

The proposal is that the federal government share the cost of providing insured services. It has never been the intention of the federal government to share in the administrative costs of a provincial plan. I beleve there is some logic in permitting a province to discharge fully the costs of admin'strat on because that will enable the province to develop the most efficient possible administration of its own plan.
If a province wishes to develop a system which involves multiple carriers, then the cost of the administration will be borne by the province itself. If it wishes to use the services of a single carrier it will benefit from this procedure. We th:nk this is a means by which a province can take full responsibility for the pattern of administration which it sets up.
It is true we are to pay 50 per cent of the *cost of the insured services in participating provinces. It may be that the provinces with lower costs will benefit to some extent. It may also be that those provinces are provinces which are less capable financially of bearing the burden of a medical care program. We Thought this was a fair procedure-paying
Medicare
half the cost of insured services in participating provinces. Thus, if there are three provinces in the plan in the beginning, the federal contribution would be based on the average of the cost to those three provinces. Conceivably, there might be three high cost provinces in the plan initially. On the other hand there might be low cost provinces. But the federal government would pay half the average per capita cost of insured services in those provinces.

maintopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
This is a very important point in respect of making payments to provinces. I recognize the minister's difficulty in that I do not think it is possible to work out all the details in this bill, but it seems to me the minister will have to determine, under some regulation, whether or not payments for services rendered by medical practitioners will apply if those medical practitioners are in the employ of a provincial government.
If the minister does not agree that services rendered by practitioners who are in the employ of a provincial government should be covered, this will discriminate against those provinces which have set up fairly extensive government health services which, in many cases, provide much better care than could be provided on an individual basis. The hon. member for Saskatoon has referred to cancer services. This is one example where in some provinces it is not possible to get a high quality service unless there is established a cancer commission and cancer clinics that guarantee incomes, research and the kind of facilities that cannot be set up in a smaller community by individual practitioners. If those practitioners and the services they provide are not going to be paid for under this plan, then of course the provinces will naturally be inclined to discontinue them.
Another example of this would be pyschia-tric care which is provided in some instances by provincial government psychiatric clinics. These services are provided by the clinics, but the practitioner is paid by the government of the province. It seems to me the province should be able to recover those expenditures under this plan.
In some provinces, and I am thinking particularly of Saskatchewan, services for the treatment of tuberculosis is provided by the anti-T.B. league, whose expenditures are met by grants from the provincial government, contributions from the general public and the sale of Easter seals and so on. If the services provided by a practitioner hired by the antituberculosis league are not going to be allowed, then certainly there will be a very strong inclination to discontinue those services. I do not think the private individual practitioner could provide the quality of service now being provided.
I am not asking the minister to change the bill because I think that would be too complicated. I hope, however, that when the minister has to determine whether or not the services provided by a medical practitioner shall be paid for he will decide to pay for the services whether the medical practitioner is in

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand the curiosity of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who has asked a legitimate question, because clause 8 of the bill does not, as he says, do anything more than express an
Medicare
intention. However, the clause has a very definite purpose and perhaps for that reason the committee will allow me to make a short statement about that purpose.
Clause 8 provides for a review in 1973 of the method by which the provinces are compensated for the federal government's share of medicare expenditures. This provision is designed to apply to medicare the general apporach which the government has adopted in respect of federal-provincial programs in the health and welfare field. Hon. members will recall that this approach was outlined to the tax structure committee on September 14, 1966.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I said then on behalf of the federal government that federal-provincial programs had been an important vehicle for bringing into existence Canada-wide programs in the field of health and welfare, and that some such vehicle would be required if new social and economic advances were to be made in the future. The medical care bill is an example of such a nation-wide advance.
During the period that programs such as hospitalization and medicare are being established and consolidated, federal contributions must be based on the actual costs of the programs. This method of compensation ensures that the federal government shares the rising costs of the programs as and where they are established, and provides an equitable basis for determining the contributions to the different provinces. It requires, of course, a reasonably uniform basis for determining the costs in the different provinces.
When the medical care programs are firmly established, however, and can properly be classed with hospitalization as continuing programs, we would propose to change the method of compensation, as we have offered to do with respect to the hospitalization programs. We would estimate that this would occur about five years after the programs had been started. Our purpose would be to ensure that federal contributions would not come to have a continuing influence over provincial decision-making, in particular over budget decisions. The new compensation would take the form of a tax transfer, equalized under the general revenue equalization formula, combined with a program equalization payment which would be calculated and escalated in such a way as to ensure that the provinces were fairly compensated. However, this program equalization payment would not be escalated by reference to the program costs:

December 6, 1966
Medicare
some other, or neutral factor would be chosen, thus rendering unnecessary the continuing reporting and auditing of provincial program costs.
I should note, Mr. Chairman, that this is the first time that legislation concerning federal-provincial programs has contained a provision concerning the form and amount of compensation after the termination date of the proposed arrangements or agreements. We consider this to be appropriate both as a method of indicating to the provinces that there is no intention of cutting off federal contributions in respect of the program, and as a method of integrating our views as to the manner in which a federal-provincial program such as this should be handled in the longer run. .Hon. members will recognize that this is in accord with the general approach to federal-provincial fiscal arrangements which I outlined to the tax structure committee on September 14 of this year.
In brief, Mr. Chairman, what clause 8 is intended to do is give notice that about five years from the date of inauguration of the medicare program the government will put forward proposals to the provinces for a change in the method of compensation, probably in the form of a tax transfer. It is, as we outlined to the federal-provincial conference our intention to give national leadership, to establish national standards, and then to observe as well as we can the jurisdictional responsibilities of the respective levels of government.

speechtext: Does this not point up the fact that it is rather awkward for a session of parliament to bind the activities of future governments even with respect to a matter of study? I still feel that the writing of this kind of thing into a statute is a little on the nonsensical side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
There were very great difficulties in deciding how best to indicate the intention of this government in proposing medicare legislation. We could simply have said that in our view at the end of five years there should be such a review of the method of compensation, and suggested that at that time the government of the day should bring forward proposals along the lines of those I placed before the federal-provincial conference in connection with other established programs. That was one extreme. On the other hand, the government could have enacted now the form of a tax transfer effective five years hence. It seemed to us premature, however, to go as far as that, and quite frankly we comprised; we put in a clause that indicates the intent of parliament at the present time, which is to require the government to review the financial provisions of the act and to bring forward such proposals as at that time they consider desirable.
As I have said, this clause carries out the general policy of this government toward federal-provincial arrangements. We believe it is desirable that the federal government should not share in provincial fields indefinitely; that the function of the federal parliament in these fields is to take initiatives to establish national standards, but not to insist that the provincial governments should follow exactly the requirements of any federal government or federal parliament thereafter. We consider such a form of financial arrangement to be no longer suitable to our modern Canadian confederation. The federal-provincial proposals that I put forward on behalf of this government carried the philosophy into the field of established programs. This clause
December 6, 1966

carries the same philosophy into the field of medicare.

maintopic: MEDICARE-AUTHORIZATION OF CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARD COST OF INSURED MEDICAL CARE

I was quite concerned about this, Mr. Chairman, because the Minister of Finance has just said that the intention of the federal government should be to take the initiative in establishing national standards. From our discussion this afternoon,
Medicare
we have certainly not drawn any assurance that national standards will be set.
The minister of health and welfare has admitted that the costs involved will not be standardized, and neither will the medical services. So now, almost at the end of the clause by clause study of this bill, the only significant thing that has been revealed has been that this bill as drawn will not give a uniform standard of medicare services to all Canadians, nor will it be conducive to uniform cost of services which will be met by the taxpayers in each of the respective provinces or territories. I think this is a shame. It is a very poor example of the type of legislation that the people of Canada expect and need.
One can readily assume now, Mr. Chairman, that the largest taxpaying and most populous province, Ontario, will receive far less benefit per capita tax dollar expended than any other sister province. This is nothing but discrimination against a province which has to bear the bulk of the contributions that the federal government collects in the first place from the Canadian public in order to pay its share to each of the provinces. The government admitted this afternoon that those shares will not be equitable as far as the taxpayers across the country are concerned.
This is a bill to grant uniform medical services across Canada, but it is nothing but another example of deception and sham. I hope that those provinces which wish to participate in the legislation and give their people a medicare plan will realize this need, and that each province in turn will correct the inequities that are present in this bill.

Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me, my remarks will deal with the three bills because they are extremely closely related. They involve the same monument at the north corner of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories. The three bills I am introducing have all been studied carefully by the Senate, and for further details the hon. member might refer to the proceedings in the other place.
The Saskatchewan Act, the Manitoba Extension Act of 1912 and the Northwest Territories Act declare the northern boundary of the province of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the southern boundary of the Northwest Territories to be the parallel of the 60th degree of north latitude, and they also declare the northerly portion of the boundary between the province of Manitoba and the province of Saskatchewan to be the second meridian in the system of dominion land surveys. Obviously these are quite abstract concepts and it was to be expected that sooner or later the need for better definitions of these boundaries would arise.
That need has now arisen as prospectors, miners, hunters and other persons wishing to acquire or develop land or other resources need to know more precisely where the borders of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories are. It would also, of course, be of great advantage to the governments of these provinces, and of the territory, charged with the responsibility of administering or controlling development or exploitation activities to know the precise point on the ground at which their particular responsibilities begin or end.

As the Minister of Public Works answered, this was done under the authority of the British North America Act 1871 and, as the minister stated, article 3 makes it very clear that with the consent of the provinces the federal government can do this sort of thing.
I might say further that precedents have established that it now is considered necessary to introduce legislation in the parliament of Canada to confirm the boundaries between provinces and territories. You do not have it along the eastern Atlantic coast, for the maritime provinces, nor do we have it in British Columbia, along the Pacific coast. Reference is made, for example, to investments in equipment amounting to $65 million. Surely, this equipment will last longer than a year and yet it is to be financed out of taxes collected in a single year although it will remain as completely paid assets in 1968, 1969, 1970. It is out of our taxes collected in a single year that such expenses will be made
Well, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that in principle, no company and no business man would proceed in this way.
The Canadian National Railways and the government take the liberty of doing this because they are using the people's taxes, and it is the people who will be taxed in order to enable the Canadian National Railways to purchase equipment. What we should do is let the Canadian National Railways purchase their equipment, borrow accordingly, and, in return, give, the C.N.R. the opportunity to collect the necessary money in order to repay the loan progressively by means of a sinking fund. This is how any company, operating in a normal manner, would proceed. But this is not how we proceed; we prefer to let the taxpayers carry the whole burden. And what is the final result of this procedure? Well, the Canadian National Railways, once it has purchased all its equipment, having no debt to pay, not having to take certain sums out of its operating fund for debts, can afford to reduce its rates. But at whose expense? At the expense of competing companies, for instance, the trucking and bus companies, etc. And who pays for all this? It is the Canadian taxpayer who pays to have the Canadian National Railway, a crown corporation, compete illegally in the field of freight or public transportation.
Now then, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the principle of this bill whose purpose it is to authorize the C.N.R. to purchase land and equipment and not be made to pay for this land or equipment out of profits realized by use of the land or the equipment which would be perfectly normal-but whereby the Canadian citizens' taxes are going to pay the cost.

Mr. Speaker, in principle, I am not against authorizing the C.N.R. to borrow or issue bonds for its own development; on the contrary, development of our transport companies, the C.N.R., Air Canada, etc., should be encouraged.
If the Canadian National Railways are allowed to make capital expenditures but do not have the necessary funds, let them borrow according to the capital expenditures they are authorized to make, for these capital expenditures, which come to $161 million, represent an additional asset for the Canadian National Railways. If the C.N.R. builds branch lines, improves hotels, buys rolling stock, or invests money in other companies and in affiliated companies, their assets will be increased.
Therefore I do not object to the Canadian National Railways borrowing in order to improve or increase its assets, I object when they are told: Increase your assets but, to finance them, we will have to use the taxpayers money. As far as I am concerned, I would rather have them told: Increase your assets, and with your profits you will pay for equipment or the capital expenditures that you are making at present.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are two items on the order paper with which we do not intend to proceed. One is item 108, a motion for concurrence in the twelfth report of the standing committee on transport and communications. Since that committee has finished its work and reported to the house, this motion becomes redundant and unnecessary. The other is item No. 23 on the order paper, the house again in committee of the whole on a bill to incorporate the Ottawa Terminal Railway Company. The purposes for which that bill was proposed have been taken care of by agreement, so the bill has become unnecessary. Therefore it is no longer intended to proceed with it. I would ask the permission of the house to drop those two items from the order paper.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while I have no objection to dropping Bill S-2, we on this side of the house would be glad to pass it through all stages tonight if the minister would call it.
